It remains to identify this common risk.  Assumption (mathrm{ass{:}observed  ext{-}margin}) and the definition of (r_{a,x}) imply
\[
r_{a,x}=\widetilde P(Y=1\mid A=a,X=x).
\]
Assumption (mathrm{ass{:}consistency}) replaces (Y) by (Y(a)) on ({A=a}), while Assumption (mathrm{ass{:}latent  ext{-}ignorability}) removes (A) from the conditional potential-outcome distribution given ((X,U)).  The law of total probability therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_{a,x}
&=\widetilde P\{Y(a)=1\mid A=a,X=x\}\\
&=\sum_{u=0}^1
  \widetilde P\{Y(a)=1\mid A=a,U=u,X=x\}
  \widetilde P(U=u\mid A=a,X=x)\\
&=\sum_{u=0}^1
  \mu_{a,u,x}\widetilde P(U=u\mid A=a,X=x)\\
&=\mu_{a,0,x}\sum_{u=0}^1
  \widetilde P(U=u\mid A=a,X=x)
=\mu_{a,0,x}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All displayed conditional probabilities and all divisions used above are well defined because (widetilde P) lies in the strictly positive class; in particular, every ((A=a,U=u,X=x)) cell has positive mass.  We have proved, for every ((a,x)),
\[
\mu_{a,0,x}=\mu_{a,1,x}=r_{a,x}.
\]
Equivalently, (  heta_{a,x}=1) on the strictly positive chart.  This conclusion also follows through the mixture parameterization: Definition (mathrm{def{:}mixture  ext{-}root}) and Lemma (mathrm{lem{:}binary  ext{-}mixture  ext{-}inversion}) give
\[
\kappa(r_{a,x},w_{a,x},1)=r_{a,x},
\qquad m_0=m_1=r_{a,x}.
\]
Since the interval ([Gamma_a^{-1},Gamma_a]) is now the singleton ({1}), Definition (mathrm{def{:}adjusted  ext{-}arm  ext{-}mean}) yields, for every strictly positive feasible posterior pair,
\[
q_{a,x}(w_0,w_1;1)
=r_{a,x}+(\pi_x-w_{a,x})(r_{a,x}-r_{a,x})
=r_{a,x}.
\]
It follows from Definition (mathrm{def{:}common  ext{-}u  ext{-}endpoints}) that
\[
H^-_x(w_0,w_1)=H^+_x(w_0,w_1)=r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}
\]
on the strictly positive part of (D_{A,x}).  Proposition (mathrm{prop{:}closed  ext{-}chart  ext{-}extension}) extends both objectives continuously to all of the compact region (D_{A,x}), including the constant-(U) corners.  Every boundary pair is a limit of strictly positive feasible pairs; hence continuity preserves the displayed constant value on all of (D_{A,x}).  Therefore
\[
\ell_x=\upsilon_x=r_{1,x}-r_{0,x},
\qquad
L=R=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\lambda_x(r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}).
\]
Finally, (w_{0,x}=w_{1,x}=1/2) is strictly positive and feasible.  Theorem (mathrm{thm{:}sharp  ext{-}common  ext{-}u  ext{-}envelope}) identifies the images of both (mathcal M^{\circ}(P_{\mathrm{obs}},\Gamma_A,1,1)) and its closed extension with ([L,R]).  Thus the displayed singleton is the exact, interior-attained ATE identified set in the second regime as well.

statements.statement: Let all three budgets diverge and allow a sequence of compatible laws with \(w_{1,x}\to1\), \(w_{0,x}\to0\), \(\widetilde P(A=1\mid U=1,X=x)\to1\), and \(\widetilde P(A=1\mid U=0,X=x)\to0\).  Then \([L,R]\) converges to the binary-outcome Manski interval \(\left[\sum_x\lambda_x\{p_xr_{1,x}-(1-p_x)r_{0,x}-p_x\},\;\sum_x\lambda_x\{p_xr_{1,x}-(1-p_x)r_{0,x}+1-p_x\}\right]\).  No Manski-recovery claim is made at finite budgets or under latent positivity bounded away from zero.
statements.justification: The all-budget limit locates the model between point identification and unrestricted treatment-response bounds without overstating finite-budget coverage.
statements.gap: Imbens relates unrestricted sensitivity to worst-case bounds qualitatively; this proposition gives the exact common-binary-\(U\) endpoint limit and the required loss of latent positivity.
statements.consumer: Users can interpret very large budgets against a familiar worst-case benchmark and detect implementations that converge to the wrong limit.
statements.proof_tex:
Let \(n\mapsto(\Gamma_{A,n},\Gamma_{0,n},\Gamma_{1,n})\) be a sequence in \([1,\infty)^3\) such that every coordinate tends to infinity, and let \(L_n,R_n\) denote the functionals in \(\mathrm{def{:}common\text{-}u\text{-}endpoints}\) evaluated at these budgets.  We prove convergence of the two endpoints.

First we derive a budget-free outer bound by worst-case completion of the two unobserved treatment-response means.  Fix \(x\in\mathcal X\).  For a compatible full-data law put
\[
 s_{1,x}=\widetilde E\{Y(1)\mid A=0,X=x\},
 \qquad
 s_{0,x}=\widetilde E\{Y(0)\mid A=1,X=x\}.
\]
The conditions \(0<p_x<1\) and \(\lambda_x>0\) make these conditional expectations well defined, and binary outcomes imply \(0\leq s_{a,x}\leq1\).  Observed-law compatibility and consistency give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \widetilde E\{Y(1)\mid X=x\}
   &=p_xr_{1,x}+(1-p_x)s_{1,x},\\
 \widetilde E\{Y(0)\mid X=x\}
   &=(1-p_x)r_{0,x}+p_xs_{0,x}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
 b_x^-:=p_xr_{1,x}-(1-p_x)r_{0,x}-p_x
 \leq \widetilde E\{Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x\}
 \leq p_xr_{1,x}-(1-p_x)r_{0,x}+1-p_x=:b_x^+.
 \tag{1}
\]
The observed-margin and consistency restrictions are closed equalities in the finite-dimensional cell probabilities.  Thus (1) also holds for every law in the closure \(\mathcal M\) from \(\mathrm{def{:}common\text{-}u\text{-}class}\).  Since \(\mathrm{thm{:}sharp\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}envelope}\) identifies \([L_n,R_n]\) with the exact image of \(\tau\) over that closed class, weighting (1) by \(\lambda_x\) and summing over the finite set \(\mathcal X\) yields
\[
 B^-:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\lambda_xb_x^-
 \leq L_n\leq R_n\leq
 \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\lambda_xb_x^+=:B^+.
 \tag{2}
\]

We next give feasible common-confounder sequences approaching both inequalities in (2).  Define
\[
 \varepsilon_n=\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{\Gamma_{A,n}}},
 \qquad
 w_{1,x}^{(n)}=1-\varepsilon_n,
 \qquad
 w_{0,x}^{(n)}=\varepsilon_n
 \tag{3}
\]
for every \(x\).  These prevalences lie in \((0,1)\), converge respectively to one and zero, and satisfy
\[
 \frac{w_{1,x}^{(n)}(1-w_{0,x}^{(n)})}
      {w_{0,x}^{(n)}(1-w_{1,x}^{(n)})}
 =\left(\frac{1-\varepsilon_n}{\varepsilon_n}\right)^2
 =\Gamma_{A,n}.
 \tag{4}
\]
Hence (3) belongs to \(D_{A,x}\): the upper treatment-odds inequality is an equality and the lower one follows from \(\Gamma_{A,n}^{-1}\leq\Gamma_{A,n}\).  Its marginal confounder prevalence is
\[
 \pi_x^{(n)}=p_x(1-\varepsilon_n)+(1-p_x)\varepsilon_n\longrightarrow p_x.
 \tag{5}
\]
Bayes' formula, whose denominators are positive by (3) and \(0<p_x<1\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \widetilde P_n(A=1\mid U=1,X=x)
 &=\frac{p_x(1-\varepsilon_n)}
         {p_x(1-\varepsilon_n)+(1-p_x)\varepsilon_n}
 \longrightarrow1,\\
 \widetilde P_n(A=1\mid U=0,X=x)
 &=\frac{p_x\varepsilon_n}
         {p_x\varepsilon_n+(1-p_x)(1-\varepsilon_n)}
 \longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]
This verifies explicitly the asserted loss of latent treatment positivity.

For \(a\in\{0,1\}\), a positive number \(\vartheta\), and the posterior prevalence \(w_{a,x}^{(n)}\), set
\[
 m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)
   =\kappa(r_{a,x},w_{a,x}^{(n)},\vartheta),
 \qquad
 m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)
   =\frac{\vartheta m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)}
          {1+(\vartheta-1)m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)}.
 \tag{7}
\]
Binary-mixture inversion, as incorporated in the sharp-envelope result, shows that both risks are in \((0,1)\) and that
\[
 r_{a,x}=(1-w_{a,x}^{(n)})m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)
          +w_{a,x}^{(n)}m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta),
 \qquad
 \frac{m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)}
      {1-m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)}
 =\vartheta
  \frac{m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)}
       {1-m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)}.
 \tag{8}
\]
The positivity of the four denominators in (8) follows from the interior-risk conclusion.

We now establish the needed limits directly from (8).  If \(w_{a,x}^{(n)}\to1\), then
\[
 \left|m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta_n)-r_{a,x}\right|
 =(1-w_{a,x}^{(n)})
  \left|m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta_n)
        -m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta_n)\right|
 \leq1-w_{a,x}^{(n)}.
 \tag{9}
\]
If \(w_{a,x}^{(n)}\to0\), the analogous identity gives
\[
 \left|m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta_n)-r_{a,x}\right|
 \leq w_{a,x}^{(n)}.
 \tag{10}
\]
Because \(r_{a,x}\in(0,1)\), equations (8)--(10), continuity of the odds map on \((0,1)\), and divergence of the outcome budgets imply that on the lower branch \(\vartheta_{a,n}=\Gamma_{a,n}\),
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 m_{1,1,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{1,n})\longrightarrow r_{1,x},
 &m_{1,0,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{1,n})\longrightarrow0,\\
 m_{0,0,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{0,n})\longrightarrow r_{0,x},
 &m_{0,1,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{0,n})\longrightarrow1.
\end{array}
\tag{11}
\]
For example, the first limit is (9), and then the second odds in (8) equal the first odds divided by \(\Gamma_{1,n}\), which tends to zero.  The control-arm limits follow from (10), after which multiplication of the limiting positive finite odds by \(\Gamma_{0,n}\) makes the other odds diverge.  On the upper branch \(\vartheta_{a,n}=\Gamma_{a,n}^{-1}\), the same calculation gives
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 m_{1,1,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{1,n}^{-1})\longrightarrow r_{1,x},
 &m_{1,0,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{1,n}^{-1})\longrightarrow1,\\
 m_{0,0,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{0,n}^{-1})\longrightarrow r_{0,x},
 &m_{0,1,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{0,n}^{-1})\longrightarrow0.
\end{array}
\tag{12}
\]

It remains to verify that these algebraic branches are attained by compatible laws.  For each \(n\), each of the two branches, and every stratum, define the \((X,A,U)\) margin by
\[
 \widetilde P_n(X=x,A=a,U=u)
 =\lambda_xp_x^a(1-p_x)^{1-a}
  \{w_{a,x}^{(n)}\}^{u}\{1-w_{a,x}^{(n)}\}^{1-u}.
 \tag{13}
\]
Conditionally on \((X=x,U=u)\), let \(Y(0)\) and \(Y(1)\) be independent Bernoulli variables with the respective success probabilities in (7), use the same conditional law for both values of \(A\), and set \(Y=AY(1)+(1-A)Y(0)\).  Every cell of this full-data law is strictly positive because \(\lambda_x>0\), \(0<p_x<1\), (3) is interior, and all risks in (7) lie in \((0,1)\).  The construction makes \((Y(0),Y(1))\perp A\mid(X,U)\) and enforces consistency.  The mixture equality in (8) reproduces each observed risk \(r_{a,x}\), so the binary observed margin is \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\).  Equation (4) verifies both treatment-odds restrictions.  In the outcome cross-product ratio, the factors \(\lambda_x\pi_x^{(n)}\) and \(\lambda_x(1-\pi_x^{(n)})\) cancel, leaving exactly the conditional-risk odds ratio in (8), which is either \(\Gamma_{a,n}\) or \(\Gamma_{a,n}^{-1}\); thus both outcome-odds restrictions hold.  Consequently each constructed law belongs to \(\mathcal M^{\circ}\).

Under either branch its adjusted arm mean satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \widetilde E_n\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}-r_{a,x}
 &=\bigl[(1-\pi_x^{(n)})m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}
          +\pi_x^{(n)}m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}\bigr]\\
 &\quad-\bigl[(1-w_{a,x}^{(n)})m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}
          +w_{a,x}^{(n)}m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}\bigr]\\
 &=(\pi_x^{(n)}-w_{a,x}^{(n)})
   (m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}-m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}),
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
which is precisely the adjusted-arm map used by \(\mathrm{def{:}common\text{-}u\text{-}endpoints}\).  Combining (5), (11), and the first line of (14), the lower-branch stratum contrast tends to
\[
 p_xr_{1,x}-\{(1-p_x)r_{0,x}+p_x\}=b_x^-.
 \tag{15}
\]
Combining (5), (12), and (14), the upper-branch stratum contrast tends to
\[
 \{p_xr_{1,x}+1-p_x\}-(1-p_x)r_{0,x}=b_x^+.
 \tag{16}
\]
The construction is simultaneous over the finite support \(\mathcal X\), so its stratum limits may be weighted by \(\lambda_x\) and summed.  Let \(\widetilde P_n^-\) and \(\widetilde P_n^+\) denote the resulting lower- and upper-branch laws.  Their feasibility and exact sharpness give
\[
 B^-\leq L_n\leq\tau(\widetilde P_n^- )\longrightarrow B^-,
 \qquad
 B^+\geq R_n\geq\tau(\widetilde P_n^+ )\longrightarrow B^+.
\]
Thus \(L_n\to B^-\) and \(R_n\to B^+\).  Endpoint convergence is equivalent to Hausdorff convergence of these compact intervals, proving
\[
 [L_n,R_n]\longrightarrow
 \left[
 \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\lambda_x\{p_xr_{1,x}-(1-p_x)r_{0,x}-p_x\},
 \ \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\lambda_x\{p_xr_{1,x}-(1-p_x)r_{0,x}+1-p_x\}
 \right].
\]
The proof uses divergence of both outcome budgets in (11)--(12), divergence of the treatment budget in (3)--(4), and the vanishing latent propensities in (6).  It therefore establishes only the stated all-budget, vanishing-positivity limit and makes no finite-budget recovery claim.

statements.statement: Writing \(\gamma=(\Gamma_A,\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1)\), construct from \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{inf}}\) a confidence region for \(\mathfrak T_0(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\cap\mathcal B\) that is asymptotically honest uniformly along sequences approaching finite optimizer ties, legal-root collisions, and positive-dimensional stationary continua.  For every singular stratum at which the first nonzero normal term of the active lower-endpoint algebraic germ has contact order \(k\geq1\), determine the sharp local Hausdorff rate, weak limit, and leading constant, including the Gaussian minimum over tied branches and root birth or death at even \(k\).  The unique nondegenerate \(k=1\) branch with \(\nabla_\gamma L\neq0\) is excluded because it is settled by Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}regular\text{-}tipping\text{-}inference}\).
statements.justification: Population sharpness does not by itself quantify sampling uncertainty at the branch switches that define the scientifically relevant frontier.
statements.gap: Zhang--Tchetgen Tchetgen and Nabi et al. treat smooth sensitivity maps, while Fang--Santos gives generic directional theory; none handles this certified algebraic active-set geometry.
statements.consumer: Empirical investigators need coverage statements for the entire set of confounding budgets that preserve a sign conclusion, including near ties.

obligation.what_is_open: Construct a uniformly honest confidence region for the zero-tipping frontier and determine the sharp local Hausdorff rate, weak limit, and leading constant at finite optimizer ties, legal-root collisions, positive-dimensional stationary continua, and algebraic contact order \(k\geq2\).
obligation.obstruction: At a singular stratum the active feasible correspondence moves with the observed law.  A tie produces a Gaussian minimum over several germs; a collision changes the legal-root inventory; a continuum produces a Gaussian support functional indexed by a semialgebraic set; and even-order contact can create or destroy real roots.  The frozen primitives provide neither a uniform stochastic expansion of this moving correspondence nor the anti-concentration and set-inversion bounds needed for honest Hausdorff coverage.
obligation.attempted: Implicit differentiation and the asymptotically linear expansion close the unique nondegenerate branch.  Finite-minimum algebra gives the pointwise derivative at a fixed tie, and balancing a fixed order-\(k\) germ against root-\(n\) noise gives the candidate scale \(n^{-1/(2k)}\).  These arguments fail to control local sequences on which branches merge, disappear, or become a continuum.
obligation.partial_result:
Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}regular\text{-}tipping\text{-}inference}\) proves the \(k=1\) unique-branch law
\[
\sqrt n\,t_n\Longrightarrow
-\frac{\dot L_bZ}{\|\nabla_\gamma L\|},
\qquad
\operatorname{se}_{\sqrt n}(t_n)=\frac{\sigma_L}{\|\nabla_\gamma L\|}.
\]
For finitely many analytic branches \(L_j\) tied at a fixed point, the elementary finite-minimum expansion gives \(L'(h)=\min_{j\in I}\nabla L_j^{\mathsf T}h\), with a maximum in place of a minimum for an upper endpoint.  For one fixed scalar germ \(L(b_0,\gamma_0+t\nu)=ct^k+o(|t|^k)\), \(c\neq0\), balanced against an \(n^{-1/2}\) stochastic perturbation, the only possible nondegenerate displacement scale is \(n^{-1/(2k)}\), and any pointwise candidate limit must solve \(cs^k+G=0\).  These pointwise calculations do not establish uniform Hausdorff coverage, select among several moving tied germs, or handle disappearance of real roots when \(k\) is even.

statements.statement:
Write the observed summary in the nonredundant chart
\[
b=\bigl(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{J-1},(p_x,r_{0,x},r_{1,x})_{x\in\mathcal X}\bigr)\in\mathbb R^{4J-1},
\qquad
\lambda_J=1-\sum_{x<J}\lambda_x,
\]
and write \(\gamma=(\Gamma_A,\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1)\).  Let \((b_0,\gamma_0)\) have strictly positive observed cells and finite budgets, let \(\gamma_0\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal B\cap(1,\infty)^3\), and suppose \(L(b_0,\gamma_0)=0\).  Assume that, on a neighborhood of \((b_0,\gamma_0)\), the legal-candidate system used by \(\mathsf{CERT}\) and stratified by \(\mathsf{ATLAS}\) has one unique active branch for \(L\), represented by an analytic objective \(\phi(z,b,\gamma)\) and analytic equations \(F(z,b,\gamma)=0\), where \(z\in\mathbb R^d\); at its solution \(z_0\), assume that \(F_z(z_0,b_0,\gamma_0)\) is invertible, every denominator is nonzero, every inactive inequality is strict, and the branch is strictly separated in objective value from all inactive candidates.  Define
\[
\dot L_b=\phi_b-\phi_zF_z^{-1}F_b,
\qquad
\dot L_\gamma=\phi_\gamma-\phi_zF_z^{-1}F_\gamma,
\]
with all derivatives evaluated at \((z_0,b_0,\gamma_0)\), and assume \(\dot L_\gamma\neq0\).  For independent observations \(O_i=(X_i,A_i,Y_i)\sim P_{\mathrm{obs}}\), suppose an estimator \(\widehat b_n\) obeys
\[
\sqrt n(\widehat b_n-b_0)
=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi(O_i)+o_P(1)
\ \Longrightarrow\ Z\sim N(0,\Sigma),
\qquad
E\{\psi(O_i)\}=0,
\qquad
E\|\psi(O_i)\|^2<\infty.
\]
Then
\[
\sqrt n\{L(\widehat b_n,\gamma_0)-L(b_0,\gamma_0)\}
\ \Longrightarrow\ \dot L_bZ
\sim N(0,\sigma_L^2),
\qquad
\sigma_L^2=\dot L_b\Sigma\dot L_b^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Let \(\nu_0=\dot L_\gamma^{\mathsf T}/\|\dot L_\gamma\|\), and let \(t_n\) be the unique local solution of
\[
L(\widehat b_n,\gamma_0+t_n\nu_0)=0.
\]
Then \(t_n=O_P(n^{-1/2})\) and
\[
\sqrt n\,t_n
\ \Longrightarrow\
-\frac{\dot L_bZ}{\|\dot L_\gamma\|}
\sim N\!\left(0,\frac{\sigma_L^2}{\|\nabla_\gamma L(b_0,\gamma_0)\|^2}\right).
\]
Thus the root-\(n\) standard-error constant for normal displacement of the regular zero-tipping frontier \(\mathfrak T_0(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) is exactly \(\sigma_L/\|\nabla_\gamma L\|\).  If \(\sigma_L>0\), consistent plug-in estimators of \(\Sigma\), \(\dot L_b\), and \(\dot L_\gamma\) give the usual pointwise normal confidence interval for this normal coordinate.  The same conclusions hold for \(R\) after replacing \(L\), its active minimizing branch, and its derivatives by \(R\), its active maximizing branch, and its derivatives.
statements.proof_tex:
The proof uses a local analytic implicit expansion, the stated asymptotically linear representation, and a one-dimensional root expansion.  Strictly positive observed cells put \(b_0\) in the relative interior of its \((4J-1)\)-dimensional chart.  The assumption that \(\gamma_0\) is interior to \(\mathcal B\cap(1,\infty)^3\) permits two-sided perturbations of every budget coordinate.  Nonzero denominators and strict inactive inequalities persist by continuity.  The unique active branch and strict objective separation therefore give, on a sufficiently small neighborhood,
\[
 F\{z(b,\gamma),b,\gamma\}=0,
 \qquad
 L(b,\gamma)=\phi\{z(b,\gamma),b,\gamma\}.                             \tag{28}
\]

Let \(J=F_z(z_0,b_0,\gamma_0)\), which is invertible by hypothesis, write \(h=(h_b,h_\gamma)\), and put \(v=z-z_0\).  Differentiability gives
\[
 F(z_0+v,b_0+h_b,\gamma_0+h_\gamma)
 =Jv+F_bh_b+F_\gamma h_\gamma+\rho(v,h),                               \tag{29}
\]
where \(\rho(0,h)=o(\|h\|)\) and
\[
 \|\rho(v,h)-\rho(v',h)\|=o(1)\|v-v'\|
\]
uniformly as \((v,v',h)\to0\).  On a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood, the map
\[
 v\longmapsto-J^{-1}\{F_bh_b+F_\gamma h_\gamma+\rho(v,h)\}
\]
has Lipschitz constant below one and maps a ball of radius \(C\|h\|\) into itself for a sufficiently large constant \(C\).  Its iterates are Cauchy, because successive distances decrease geometrically, and their limit is the unique solution of (29) in that ball.  Hence \(v=O(\|h\|)\), and substitution in (29) gives
\[
 z(b_0+h_b,\gamma_0+h_\gamma)-z_0
 =-J^{-1}F_bh_b-J^{-1}F_\gamma h_\gamma+o(\|h\|).                      \tag{30}
\]

Expanding the second identity in (28) and substituting (30) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 L(b_0+h_b,\gamma_0+h_\gamma)-L(b_0,\gamma_0)
 &=\phi_z\{z(b_0+h_b,\gamma_0+h_\gamma)-z_0\}
   +\phi_bh_b+\phi_\gamma h_\gamma+o(\|h\|)\\
 &=\bigl(\phi_b-\phi_zF_z^{-1}F_b\bigr)h_b
   +\bigl(\phi_\gamma-\phi_zF_z^{-1}F_\gamma\bigr)h_\gamma
   +o(\|h\|)\\
 &=\dot L_bh_b+\dot L_\gamma h_\gamma+o(\|h\|).
\end{aligned}                                                           \tag{31}
\]
This proves the displayed derivative formulas.

The assumed asymptotically linear representation implies \(\widehat b_n-b_0=O_P(n^{-1/2})\).  Take \(h_b=\widehat b_n-b_0\), \(h_\gamma=0\), and use \(L(b_0,\gamma_0)=0\) in (31).  Then
\[
 \sqrt n\,L(\widehat b_n,\gamma_0)
 =\dot L_b\sqrt n(\widehat b_n-b_0)+o_P(1)
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \dot L_bZ.                                      \tag{32}
\]
Since \(Z\sim N(0,\Sigma)\),
\[
 \dot L_bZ\sim N(0,\sigma_L^2),
 \qquad \sigma_L^2=\dot L_b\Sigma\dot L_b^{\mathsf T}.               \tag{33}
\]

For the frontier displacement, define
\[
 \nu_0=\frac{\dot L_\gamma^{\mathsf T}}{\|\dot L_\gamma\|}.
\]
The nonzero-gradient assumption gives
\[
 \dot L_\gamma\nu_0=\|\dot L_\gamma\|=:c>0.                         \tag{34}
\]
By continuity of the branch derivative, \(t\mapsto L(b,\gamma_0+t\nu_0)\) has derivative at least \(c/2\) for all sufficiently small \((b-b_0,t)\).  Choose deterministic \(M_n\to\infty\) with \(M_n/\sqrt n\to0\).  Equation (32) implies that, with probability tending to one,
\[
 |L(\widehat b_n,\gamma_0)|<\frac{cM_n}{4\sqrt n}.
\]
The mean-value inequality makes the values at \(t=-M_n/\sqrt n\) and \(t=M_n/\sqrt n\) have opposite signs.  Continuity and strict monotonicity therefore give the unique local root \(t_n\), and a second application of the mean-value inequality gives
\[
 |t_n|\leq\frac{2}{c}|L(\widehat b_n,\gamma_0)|=O_P(n^{-1/2}).          \tag{35}
\]

Use \(h_b=\widehat b_n-b_0\) and \(h_\gamma=t_n\nu_0\) in (31).  Equations (34)--(35) make the remainder \(o_P(n^{-1/2})\), so the root equation becomes
\[
 0=\dot L_b(\widehat b_n-b_0)+\|\dot L_\gamma\|t_n+o_P(n^{-1/2}).     \tag{36}
\]
Multiplication by \(\sqrt n\), solution for \(\sqrt n t_n\), and (32) yield
\[
 \sqrt n\,t_n
 \ \Longrightarrow\
 -\frac{\dot L_bZ}{\|\dot L_\gamma\|}
 \sim N\!\left(0,\frac{\sigma_L^2}{\|\dot L_\gamma\|^2}\right).    \tag{37}
\]
Equation (31) identifies \(\dot L_\gamma=\nabla_\gamma L(b_0,\gamma_0)\), so the standard-error constant is \(\sigma_L/\|\nabla_\gamma L\|\).  If \(\sigma_L>0\), consistency of the stated plug-in estimators and continuity of matrix multiplication, the Euclidean norm, and division by the nonzero denominator give the usual pointwise normal interval.  Replacing the active minimizing branch and \(L\) by the active maximizing branch and \(R\) repeats (28)--(37), proving the final assertion.

statements.statement:
Fix \(x\in\mathcal X\) and finite budgets \(1\leq\Gamma_A,\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1<\infty\).  When \(\Gamma_A>1\), define
\[
 W_{\Gamma_A}(t)=\frac{\Gamma_A t}{1+(\Gamma_A-1)t},\; 0\leq t\leq1.
\]
For \(a\in\{0,1\}\) and \(1<\Gamma_a<\infty\), let
\[
 z_{a,\Gamma_a}(w)=\kappa(r_{a,x},w,\Gamma_a),\;
 \Delta_{a,\Gamma_a}(w)=
 \frac{\Gamma_a z_{a,\Gamma_a}(w)}
      {1+(\Gamma_a-1)z_{a,\Gamma_a}(w)}-z_{a,\Gamma_a}(w),
\]
and set \(\Delta_{a,1}(w)=0\).  For \(0<w<1\) and \(\Gamma_a>1\),
\[
 -\frac{\Delta_{a,\Gamma_a}(w)}{w}
 <\frac{d}{dw}\Delta_{a,\Gamma_a}(w)
 <\frac{\Delta_{a,\Gamma_a}(w)}{1-w}.
\]
If \(\Gamma_A>1\) and \((\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1)\neq(1,1)\), then on \(0<w_1<w_0<1\), with \(e=w_0-w_1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_x^+(w_0,w_1)
 &=r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}
 +e\{(1-p_x)\Delta_{1,\Gamma_1}(w_1)
       +p_x\Delta_{0,\Gamma_0}(w_0)\},\\
H_x^-(w_0,w_1)
 &=r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}
 -e\{(1-p_x)\Delta_{1,\Gamma_1}(1-w_1)
       +p_x\Delta_{0,\Gamma_0}(1-w_0)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently \(H_x^+\) is strictly increasing in \(w_0\) and strictly decreasing in \(w_1\), whereas \(H_x^-\) is strictly decreasing in \(w_0\) and strictly increasing in \(w_1\).  Neither relevant extremum over \(D_{A,x}\) has a two-dimensional interior optimizer, every non-point-identified optimizer saturates a treatment-odds inequality, complementing \(U\) maps every forward-arc optimizer to a reverse-arc optimizer with the same objective value, and
\[
 \ell_x=\min_{0\leq t\leq1}H_x^-(W_{\Gamma_A}(t),t),
 \;
 \upsilon_x=\max_{0\leq t\leq1}H_x^+(W_{\Gamma_A}(t),t).
\]
If \(\Gamma_A=1\) or \(\Gamma_0=\Gamma_1=1\), then instead
\(\ell_x=\upsilon_x=r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}\).
statements.proof_tex:
Fix the stratum and suppress its index.  The proof uses implicit differentiation, strict coordinate monotonicity, and the involution that relabels the two states of \(U\).

First take \(r\in(0,1)\), \(\vartheta>1\), and \(0<w<1\).  Put
\[
 f(z)=\frac{\vartheta z}{1+(\vartheta-1)z},
 \; z(w)=\kappa(r,w,\vartheta),
 \; \Delta(w)=f\{z(w)\}-z(w).
 \tag{16}
\]
Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}binary\text{-}mixture\text{-}inversion}\) gives \(0<z(w)<f\{z(w)\}<1\) and
\[
 r=(1-w)z(w)+wf\{z(w)\}=z(w)+w\Delta(w).
 \tag{17}
\]
Because
\[
 f'(z)=\frac{\vartheta}{\{1+(\vartheta-1)z\}^2}>0,
 \;
 D(w)=1-w+wf'\{z(w)\}>0,
 \tag{18}
\]
the derivative of the left side of the mixture equation with respect to \(z\) is nonzero.  Implicit differentiation is therefore legal and yields
\[
 z'(w)=-\frac{\Delta(w)}{D(w)},
 \;
 \Delta'(w)=\{f'\{z(w)\}-1\}z'(w).
 \tag{19}
\]
Combining (18)--(19), equation by equation, gives
\[
 \Delta(w)+w\Delta'(w)=\frac{\Delta(w)}{D(w)}>0,
 \;
 \Delta(w)-(1-w)\Delta'(w)
 =\frac{\Delta(w)f'\{z(w)\}}{D(w)}>0.
 \tag{20}
\]
Division in (20) is valid because \(0<w<1\), and it proves
\[
 -\frac{\Delta(w)}{w}<\Delta'(w)
 <\frac{\Delta(w)}{1-w}.
 \tag{21}
\]
This proves the asserted derivative inequalities for every nontrivial arm budget.  The convention \(\Delta_{a,1}=0\) covers a trivial arm without applying the strict inequalities to it.

We next record the relabeling identity.  For a posterior pair \(d=(w_0,w_1)\), define
\[
 d^c=(1-w_0,1-w_1),\quad \pi^c=1-\pi.
 \tag{22}
\]
If \((m_0,m_1)\) is the unique feasible risk pair at mixture weight \(w_a\) and odds ratio \(\vartheta\), then \((m_1,m_0)\) is feasible at weight \(1-w_a\) and odds ratio \(\vartheta^{-1}\).  Indeed,
\[
 w_am_1+(1-w_a)m_0=r_{a,x},
 \;
 \operatorname{OR}(m_0,m_1)=\vartheta^{-1}.
 \tag{23}
\]
Uniqueness in Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}binary\text{-}mixture\text{-}inversion}\) therefore identifies this as the pair used by the adjusted-arm map.  Since
\[
 \pi^c-(1-w_a)=-(\pi-w_a),
 \; m_0-m_1=-(m_1-m_0),
\]
Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}adjusted\text{-}arm\text{-}mean}\) gives
\[
 q_{a,x}(d^c;\vartheta^{-1})=q_{a,x}(d;\vartheta).
 \tag{24}
\]
The endpoint set \(\{\Gamma_a^{-1},\Gamma_a\}\) is invariant under reciprocation.  Hence
\[
 q_{a,x}^{\pm}(d^c)=q_{a,x}^{\pm}(d),
 \; H_x^{\pm}(d^c)=H_x^{\pm}(d).
 \tag{25}
\]
The two cross-product inequalities defining \(D_{A,x}\) are also exchanged by \(d\mapsto d^c\), so this involution preserves the exposure region and maps its forward half to its reverse half.

Now suppose \(0<w_1<w_0<1\) and put \(e=w_0-w_1\).  The definition of \(\pi\) gives
\[
 \pi-w_1=(1-p_x)e>0,
 \; \pi-w_0=-p_xe<0,
 \tag{26}
\]
where strictness uses the observed overlap condition \(0<p_x<1\).  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}outcome\text{-}budget\text{-}extrema}\), followed by (24) for the reciprocal tilt, gives
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
q^+_{1,x}=r_{1,x}+(1-p_x)e\Delta_{1,\Gamma_1}(w_1),
&q^-_{1,x}=r_{1,x}-(1-p_x)e\Delta_{1,\Gamma_1}(1-w_1),\\
q^-_{0,x}=r_{0,x}-p_xe\Delta_{0,\Gamma_0}(w_0),
&q^+_{0,x}=r_{0,x}+p_xe\Delta_{0,\Gamma_0}(1-w_0).
\end{array}
\tag{27}
\]
Subtracting the appropriate two entries proves the two displayed formulas in the statement.

Write
\[
 B=(1-p_x)\Delta_{1,\Gamma_1}(w_1)
   +p_x\Delta_{0,\Gamma_0}(w_0).
\]
At least one summand is strictly positive because \((\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1)\neq(1,1)\).  Since \(e<w_0\), the lower inequality in (21) gives
\[
 \frac{\partial H_x^+}{\partial w_0}
 =B+ep_x\Delta'_{0,\Gamma_0}(w_0)
 >(1-p_x)\Delta_{1,\Gamma_1}(w_1)
   +p_x\Delta_{0,\Gamma_0}(w_0)\left(1-\frac e{w_0}\right)>0.
 \tag{28}
\]
Terms belonging to an arm with \(\Gamma_a=1\) are simply zero.  Since \(e<1-w_1\), the upper inequality in (21) similarly gives
\[
 \frac{\partial H_x^+}{\partial w_1}
 =-B+e(1-p_x)\Delta'_{1,\Gamma_1}(w_1)
 <-p_x\Delta_{0,\Gamma_0}(w_0)
  -(1-p_x)\Delta_{1,\Gamma_1}(w_1)
       \left(1-\frac e{1-w_1}\right)<0.
 \tag{29}
\]

For the lower objective put
\[
 C=(1-p_x)\Delta_{1,\Gamma_1}(1-w_1)
   +p_x\Delta_{0,\Gamma_0}(1-w_0).
\]
Using respectively \(e<w_0\), the upper inequality in (21) at \(1-w_0\), \(e<1-w_1\), and the lower inequality in (21) at \(1-w_1\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac{\partial H_x^-}{\partial w_0}
 &=-C+ep_x\Delta'_{0,\Gamma_0}(1-w_0)\\
 &<-(1-p_x)\Delta_{1,\Gamma_1}(1-w_1)
   -p_x\Delta_{0,\Gamma_0}(1-w_0)\left(1-\frac e{w_0}\right)<0,\\
 \frac{\partial H_x^-}{\partial w_1}
 &=C+e(1-p_x)\Delta'_{1,\Gamma_1}(1-w_1)\\
 &>p_x\Delta_{0,\Gamma_0}(1-w_0)
   +(1-p_x)\Delta_{1,\Gamma_1}(1-w_1)
       \left(1-\frac e{1-w_1}\right)>0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{30}
\]
Thus no relevant optimizer lies in the two-dimensional interior of either half of \(D_{A,x}\).

For an interior reverse-half point, the exposure inequalities are equivalent to
\[
 w_1\leq w_0\leq W_{\Gamma_A}(w_1).
 \tag{31}
\]
If the upper inequality is strict, increasing \(w_0\) to \(W_{\Gamma_A}(w_1)\) remains feasible; by (28) it strictly raises \(H_x^+\), and by (30) it strictly lowers \(H_x^-\).  Hence the upper maximizer and lower minimizer in the reverse half lie on
\[
 (w_0,w_1)=(W_{\Gamma_A}(t),t),\; 0<t<1.
 \tag{32}
\]
Equation (25) carries every forward-half candidate to the reverse half without changing either objective.  On the diagonal and at the constant-confounder corners, \(\pi=w_0=w_1\), so \(H_x^-=H_x^+=r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}\).  For every \(0<t<1\), however, \(W_{\Gamma_A}(t)>t\), and (27) makes \(H_x^+\) strictly larger and \(H_x^-\) strictly smaller than this diagonal value.  Therefore no diagonal point or constant-\(U\) corner is optimal in the non-point-identified case.  Continuity at \(t=0,1\), supplied by Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}closed\text{-}chart\text{-}extension}\), now proves the two one-dimensional endpoint formulas and shows that their optimizers actually have \(0<t<1\).

Finally, if \(\Gamma_A=1\), the two exposure inequalities imply \(w_0=w_1\), whence \(\pi=w_a\) and every adjusted arm mean equals \(r_{a,x}\).  If \(\Gamma_0=\Gamma_1=1\), both outcome tilts equal one, so the two latent risks in each arm are equal and again every adjusted arm mean equals its observed arm risk.  In either case \(\ell_x=\upsilon_x=r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}\), as claimed.
statements.justification: Strict tilt-gap derivatives collapse each non-point-identified two-dimensional exposure optimization to one canonical odds-boundary arc.
statements.gap: The fixed-tuple binary-confounder comparator does not supply this common-posterior endpoint reduction, and no historical class transfer is asserted.
statements.consumer: The sharp envelope, fixed-input certificate, parametric tipping atlas, and strict-gap witness can enumerate one exposure arc and recover the other by relabeling \(U\).
